content.title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
content.specialty: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine and Cardiology

redFlags: Blood pressure at or above the severe range with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, acute kidney injury or heart failure
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy with severe hypertension or concerning symptoms
Acute focal neurological deficit or aortic-dissection features
Suspected catecholamine crisis or another rapidly progressive secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic and detected on screening
Headache or dizziness, which are non-specific
Symptoms of target-organ disease such as exertional chest discomfort, breathlessness or neurological episodes
Features suggesting a secondary cause, including episodic palpitations, muscle weakness or sleep apnoea
physicalSigns: Repeated elevated clinic blood pressure using correct technique
Postural blood-pressure fall in older adults, diabetes or symptomatic patients
Retinal vascular change
Signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or endocrine disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Raised clinic readings with normal validated ambulatory or home averages.
Normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office averages or unexplained target-organ damage.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistant disease, hypokalaemia, renal findings, endocrine features or a medicine/substance trigger.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness or recent stimulant exposure with normal readings after the driver resolves.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure — Persistent clinic hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinic blood pressure remains at or above the diagnostic threshold after repeat measurement with correct cuff and positioning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Technique and repetition reduce random error and identify inter-arm difference.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average waking readings meet the validated diagnostic threshold using adequate measurements.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Preferred confirmation method for clinic readings below the severe range and distinguishes white-coat effect.

ruleIn.testName: Home blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average readings after discarding the first day meet the validated home threshold.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides confirmation and supports later self-monitoring when performed with a validated device and protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis — Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No albuminuria or haematuria, or an abnormality prompts renal evaluation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Renal disease can be both a cause and consequence of hypertension and changes treatment choice and targets.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile — Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Baseline metabolic and renal status is defined; hypokalaemia, kidney dysfunction or diabetes redirects assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports cardiovascular-risk estimation and safe medicine selection.

ruleOut.testName: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram — Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No hypertensive retinopathy or left-ventricular/cardiac abnormality, or damage is documented for risk management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Target-organ damage changes urgency and the balance of treatment benefit.

pathophysiology.summary: Sustained arterial hypertension reflects increased systemic vascular resistance, altered sodium-volume balance and neurohormonal activation interacting with age, genetics, adiposity and environmental exposures. Chronic pressure load accelerates vascular remodelling and damages the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and peripheral arteries.
keyMechanisms: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation increase vascular tone and sodium retention.
Endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness raise systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
Renal sodium handling and pressure natriuresis reset at a higher arterial pressure.
Persistent load causes left-ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy and cerebrovascular injury.

clinicalManagement.title: Measure and confirm
actions: Use a validated, maintained device, correct cuff size, supported arm and a quiet seated setting.
Measure both arms initially and use the arm with the persistently higher reading.
Confirm clinic hypertension with ambulatory monitoring or, when unsuitable, structured home monitoring unless urgent severe hypertension requires immediate assessment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At initial and confirmation visits

clinicalManagement.title: Identify severe hypertension requiring urgent assessment
actions: Assess for retinal, neurological, cardiac, aortic and renal target-organ injury.
Use emergency transfer for life-threatening symptoms or suspected acute organ injury.
Do not rapidly lower asymptomatic blood pressure outside a monitored, indication-specific protocol.
Activate emergency specialist management and monitored intravenous therapy under the local protocol.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure with acute target-organ injury

actions: Arrange urgent clinical review, confirm adherence and complete prompt organ assessment rather than routine follow-up.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure without acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day when severe readings or symptoms are present

clinicalManagement.title: Assess cardiovascular risk and organ damage
actions: Obtain urine albumin-creatinine ratio, haematuria screen, glycated haemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR and lipids.
Perform fundoscopy and a 12-lead electrocardiogram.
Use a cardiovascular-risk tool validated or approved for local Saudi practice and assess for secondary-cause clues.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During diagnostic confirmation

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifestyle and pharmacological treatment
actions: Offer lifestyle intervention to every patient and discuss medicine using age, diabetes, kidney disease, pregnancy potential, frailty and cardiovascular risk.
Use generic ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, calcium-channel blockers or thiazide-like diuretics in the guideline sequence when suitable and SFDA authorised.
Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin-receptor blocker.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for dose, contraindication and monitoring decisions; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After confirmed diagnosis, sooner when severity or organ damage requires

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate and monitor
actions: Check adherence, side effects, postural symptoms and validated clinic or home readings before intensification.
Monitor kidney function and electrolytes after renin-angiotensin system blockers, diuretics or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists according to protocol.
Before labelling resistant hypertension, confirm out-of-office elevation, optimal tolerated triple therapy and adherence, then seek specialist input or use protocol-directed fourth-line treatment.
Individualise targets for frailty, multimorbidity and significant postural hypotension.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At defined intervals after each treatment change and at least annually once stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review after initiation or each medicine change until a stable target is achieved, then provide at least annual review of blood pressure, postural symptoms, lifestyle, adherence, adverse effects, renal function and evolving cardiovascular risk.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care pharmacist or nurse for adherence and home-monitoring support
Nephrology, endocrinology or hypertension specialist for suspected secondary or resistant hypertension
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy, pregnancy planning or postpartum hypertension
Dietitian, weight-management and smoking-cessation services according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce dietary sodium using culturally relevant food choices; avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes when kidney disease, diabetes or interacting medicines make them unsafe.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity and gradual weight reduction when indicated.
Limit excessive caffeine and alcohol, stop smoking and address sleep apnoea risk.
Do not recommend calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements solely to lower blood pressure.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often silent but treatment reduces long-term cardiovascular and renal risk.
Teach validated home-monitoring technique and how to record readings without excessive repeated checking.
Discuss medicine purpose, common adverse effects, pregnancy precautions and when to seek urgent care.
dischargeCriteria: Hypertension is confirmed or excluded using an appropriate out-of-office pathway.
Target-organ and cardiovascular-risk assessment is complete or has a named owner.
Treatment, monitoring, individual target and urgent symptom advice are documented and understood.

content.specialty: Thoracic Oncology, Respiratory Medicine and Thoracic Surgery

redFlags: Massive haemoptysis or threatened airway
Superior vena cava obstruction with respiratory or neurological compromise
Spinal-cord compression symptoms or new focal neurological deficit
Severe hypercalcaemia, pericardial tamponade or rapidly worsening respiratory failure
symptoms: Persistent or changing cough
Haemoptysis, breathlessness or chest pain
Unexplained weight loss, fatigue or recurrent focal pneumonia
Hoarseness, bone pain, headache or focal neurological symptoms
physicalSigns: Focal reduced air entry, wheeze or signs of pleural effusion
Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
Clubbing or features of superior vena cava obstruction
Neurological deficit, bony tenderness or paraneoplastic manifestations

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Epidemiologic risk, constitutional symptoms, cavitation and specific microbiological evidence.
Acute infective presentation that resolves radiographically; persistence or recurrence in one lobe raises concern for obstruction.
Stable interval imaging or benign calcification/morphology within a validated nodule pathway.
Known extrathoracic cancer and pathology/immunophenotype inconsistent with a pulmonary primary.

ruleIn.testName: Contrast-enhanced CT chest and upper abdomen
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Contrast-enhanced CT chest and upper abdomen — Primary lung malignancy and anatomical stage
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Suspicious pulmonary lesion with local, nodal or metastatic features.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Primary lung malignancy and anatomical stage
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the safest highest-yield biopsy target and initial resectability assessment.

ruleIn.testName: Image-guided, bronchoscopic or endobronchial-ultrasound biopsy
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Image-guided, bronchoscopic or endobronchial-ultrasound biopsy — Histological lung-cancer diagnosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Adequate tissue confirms histology and supports molecular and immune biomarker testing.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Tissue method should maximise diagnostic and staging value while minimising procedural risk.

ruleIn.testName: PET-CT and brain imaging when stage appropriate
ruleIn.modalityTarget: PET-CT and brain imaging when stage appropriate — Occult nodal or distant metastasis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Metabolically or anatomically suspicious disease requiring confirmation when it changes curative intent.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Prevents futile local treatment and guides invasive staging.

ruleOut.testName: Microbiology on appropriate respiratory specimens
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Microbiology on appropriate respiratory specimens — Tuberculosis or fungal infection
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No microbiological evidence of an infectious mimic, or infection is identified for treatment and isolation measures.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Infection can mimic malignancy and is especially important in cavitary disease.

ruleOut.testName: Interval nodule imaging within a validated pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Interval nodule imaging within a validated pathway — Benign or indolent pulmonary nodule
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Long-term stability or benign evolution lowers malignancy probability.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids invasive testing for appropriately selected low-risk nodules while preserving surveillance safety.

pathophysiology.summary: Lung cancer arises from malignant transformation of respiratory epithelium and is broadly classified as non-small-cell or small-cell carcinoma. Local invasion, lymphatic spread and early haematogenous dissemination determine resectability and systemic treatment; molecular drivers and immune phenotype increasingly guide therapy.
keyMechanisms: Tobacco smoke, environmental and occupational carcinogens produce cumulative genomic injury.
Histological subtype and molecular alterations determine growth pattern and treatment sensitivity.
Mediastinal nodal involvement strongly affects stage and curative options.
Metastatic spread commonly affects brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands; paraneoplastic syndromes may precede local symptoms.

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain diagnosis and full stage
actions: Choose a biopsy that provides diagnosis and the greatest staging information with acceptable risk.
Complete TNM staging and document performance status, pulmonary function and comorbidity.
Obtain adequate tissue for current molecular-driver and immune biomarker testing in eligible non-small-cell disease.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently after suspicious imaging

clinicalManagement.title: Agree treatment in thoracic MDT
actions: Include respiratory medicine, thoracic surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, radiology, pathology and supportive care.
State whether intent is curative, disease controlling or symptom focused.
Discuss clinical trials and the patient's informed preferences.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After staging and biomarker work-up

clinicalManagement.title: Treat localised disease
actions: Offer anatomical surgical resection with nodal evaluation to operable patients when oncologically appropriate.
Use definitive stereotactic or conventional radiotherapy for selected medically inoperable localised disease.
Consider peri-operative systemic therapy according to stage, histology, biomarkers and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Without avoidable delay

clinicalManagement.title: Treat locally advanced disease
actions: Assess suitability for combined-modality chemoradiotherapy or selected surgical pathways.
Use generic systemic agents and radiotherapy schedules only from the current approved oncology protocol.
Monitor pulmonary, oesophageal, haematological and immune-related toxicity.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to MDT sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Treat advanced disease and complications
actions: Select targeted therapy, immunotherapy or cytotoxic chemotherapy according to histology, molecular findings, immune phenotype and fitness.
Use palliative radiotherapy, pleural procedures, analgesia and other symptom-directed interventions early.
Escalate cord compression, major haemoptysis, severe hypercalcaemia and superior vena cava obstruction through emergency oncology pathways.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after biomarker results; immediately for oncological emergencies

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Use stage- and treatment-specific surveillance with symptom review and scheduled imaging under the thoracic MDT; monitor late pulmonary and treatment effects and re-biopsy or repeat molecular assessment when progression could alter therapy.

Encourage pulmonary rehabilitation or activity adapted to symptoms and treatment.

content.title: Sepsis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Critical Care

redFlags: Persistent hypotension or evidence of hypoperfusion after initial fluid resuscitation
New altered consciousness, rapidly increasing oxygen need or respiratory failure
Lactate elevation with clinical deterioration or oliguria
Purpura, necrotising soft-tissue features, meningism or a source needing immediate surgical control
symptoms: Fever, rigors or feeling unusually cold
New confusion, profound weakness or reduced urine output
Breathlessness, cough, dysuria, abdominal pain or another focal infection symptom
Rapid deterioration in a patient with recent infection, procedure or immunosuppression
physicalSigns: Altered mental status
Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, mottling or cool peripheries
Oliguria, tachycardia or abnormal temperature

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ischaemic symptoms, pulmonary congestion, elevated jugular venous pressure or cardiac imaging suggesting pump failure.
History of bleeding or fluid loss without a convincing infectious focus; response depends on correction of the volume deficit.
Abrupt onset after exposure with skin or mucosal findings, bronchospasm or gastrointestinal symptoms.
Sudden dyspnoea or pleuritic pain, thromboembolic risk and right-heart strain without a clear infection syndrome.

ruleIn.testName: Serum lactate with repeat trend
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum lactate with repeat trend — Tissue hypoperfusion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Elevation or failure to clear in a clinically deteriorating patient.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports severity assessment and response monitoring but must be interpreted with the whole clinical picture.

ruleIn.testName: Blood cultures and source-directed microbiology
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood cultures and source-directed microbiology — Causative infection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth or molecular detection of a plausible pathogen from blood or the suspected source.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Enables antimicrobial narrowing and source-directed care; obtain before antibiotics only when this does not cause harmful delay.

ruleIn.testName: Organ-function panel
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Organ-function panel — Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute kidney, liver, coagulation, haematological or gas-exchange abnormality.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines severity, guides support and provides a baseline for trends.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary ischaemic pattern explaining the haemodynamic state.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease can mimic or coexist with sepsis and changes fluid and vasopressor decisions.

ruleOut.testName: Source-directed imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Source-directed imaging — Non-infectious mimic or drainable focus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Imaging identifies or excludes pneumonia, obstruction, perforation, abscess or another urgent source.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Confirms anatomy and determines whether procedural source control is required.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Endothelial injury, vasodilation, capillary leak, microvascular thrombosis and cellular metabolic dysfunction can impair tissue oxygen delivery and progress to shock and multiorgan failure.
keyMechanisms: An uncontrolled inflammatory and immune response disrupts endothelial integrity and vascular tone.
Relative and absolute hypovolaemia reduce effective circulating volume.
Microcirculatory dysfunction and coagulation activation impair organ perfusion.
Myocardial depression and cellular oxygen-utilisation defects can persist despite apparently corrected blood pressure.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise sepsis and grade urgency
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion and urine output.
Record observations and identify high-risk organ dysfunction without relying on a single screening score.
Activate senior and critical-care escalation for shock or rapidly worsening physiology.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain time-critical diagnostics
actions: Measure lactate and obtain blood count, renal, liver, coagulation and glucose studies.
Take blood cultures and appropriate source specimens before antimicrobials when this can be done promptly.
Use targeted imaging to locate infection and source-control needs.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As early as possible without delaying treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Start infection and perfusion treatment
actions: Administer empiric intravenous antimicrobials selected for the suspected source, local resistance patterns, allergies and recent exposure.
Give balanced crystalloid in reassessed aliquots when hypoperfusion is present, accounting for cardiac or renal risk.
Provide oxygen and organ support according to measured need.
Start vasopressor support in a monitored setting under critical-care oversight.
Use dynamic reassessment to avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload.
branches.condition: Hypotension persists despite appropriate initial fluid

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately for shock or high-likelihood sepsis

clinicalManagement.title: Achieve source control
actions: Request surgical, interventional radiology or specialty review for drainage, debridement or device removal.
Do not defer an urgent source-control procedure solely to complete non-essential tests.
Document the source-control decision and planned timing.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently once the source is identified

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess and de-escalate
actions: Trend haemodynamics, lactate, urine output, oxygen need and organ function.
Review microbiology and narrow, change or stop antimicrobials when evidence supports it.
Reconsider the diagnosis and seek additional source control if improvement is inadequate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Continuously, with formal review after initial resuscitation

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange source-appropriate clinical review and results follow-up, reconcile antimicrobials and other medicines, screen for post-sepsis functional or psychological problems, and escalate persistent fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive change or recurrent fever.

Source-specific surgical or procedural team
Microbiology or infectious diseases for complex infection or antimicrobial stewardship
Physiotherapy, dietetics and rehabilitation after prolonged or severe illness
lifestyleAndDiet: Support nutrition, hydration and mobilisation during recovery according to swallowing and organ-function assessment.
Review indicated vaccination and infection-prevention measures after the acute episode.
Address smoking and other modifiable infection risks when clinically stable.
patientEducation: Explain the suspected source, organ effects and why treatment and monitoring are time critical.
On recovery, provide signs of recurrent infection or deterioration that require urgent assessment.
Discuss antimicrobial purpose, planned review and potential adverse effects.
dischargeCriteria: Infection source and treatment plan are established with stable physiology.
Organ dysfunction has resolved or has a safe documented outpatient plan.
Oral therapy, monitoring, follow-up and explicit return precautions are feasible and understood.

redFlags: Suspected infection with new organ dysfunction

Rapid deterioration
symptoms: Fever or low temperature

Mottled or cool peripheries
Possible source-specific infection findings

ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses a common source and guides treatment.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care Pathway

content.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care Pathway

redFlags: Altered mental status, severe dehydration, or inability to maintain intake
Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or suspected metabolic crisis
Severe hypoglycaemia or infected, ischaemic, or ulcerated foot
symptoms: May be asymptomatic and found on screening
Increased thirst, urination, or hunger
Fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections, or unintentional weight change
physicalSigns: Central adiposity or other metabolic risk features
Acanthosis nigricans in some patients
Possible peripheral sensory loss, foot lesions, or vascular disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May have rapid onset, ketosis, or insulin deficiency; investigate classification when uncertain.
Temporal association with glucocorticoids or other glucose-affecting medicines.
Pancreatic disease, endocrinopathy, or another underlying cause suggested by history or course.
Occurs during acute illness and may resolve; confirm persistent diabetes when appropriate.

ruleIn.testName: Laboratory HbA1c
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Laboratory HbA1c — Chronic hyperglycaemia consistent with diabetes
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At or above locally adopted diagnostic threshold, confirmed as required
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Estimate average glycaemia when assay and patient factors permit.

ruleIn.testName: Fasting plasma glucose
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Fasting plasma glucose — Diabetes mellitus
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At or above locally adopted diagnostic threshold, confirmed as required
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess fasting glycaemia using laboratory criteria.

ruleIn.testName: Random plasma glucose with classic symptoms or crisis
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Random plasma glucose with classic symptoms or crisis — Diabetes mellitus
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Marked hyperglycaemia meeting accepted criteria in the clinical context
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: May establish diagnosis in symptomatic patients while acute status is assessed.

ruleIn.testName: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated glomerular filtration rate
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated glomerular filtration rate — Diabetic kidney disease risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Albuminuria and/or reduced estimated filtration
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify kidney involvement and inform risk and treatment planning.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat laboratory HbA1c or plasma glucose — Persistent diabetes after borderline or discordant result
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Repeat result below diagnostic thresholds without other diagnostic evidence
ruleOut.targetCondition: Persistent diabetes after borderline or discordant result
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Resolve uncertain results and consider factors affecting HbA1c.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Blood ketones, electrolytes, renal function, and acid-base assessment when acutely unwell — Diabetic ketoacidosis or acute metabolic emergency
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No significant ketonaemia, acidosis, or related derangement
ruleOut.targetCondition: Diabetic ketoacidosis or acute metabolic emergency
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assess an acute emergency when symptoms suggest it.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Risk profile characterised for management
